caption:
Ever land on a page, fight through two pop-ups, and then get asked to pick a style and a quantity before anyone's told you why the product matters?

That's what happens on this NFC review-card store. Cookie modal first. Dismiss it, an email quiz pops up asking which "card is actually you." Dismiss that, and the cookie modal comes back. Once you're finally through, you're picking Google vs TripAdvisor vs Facebook before you've read a single benefit.

Here's what I changed and why:

1. Removed the blocking popup sequence, so the page loads straight to the product
2. Moved the price and top benefit line above the style picker (both were real and correct, just sequenced too late)
3. Kept the full benefit list and bulk-pricing table together lower down, for a buyer who's ready to compare quantities
4. Repositioned the chat bubble off the sticky CTA zone
5. Swapped the hero image for a clean shot with no competing brand in frame
6. Added a return/guarantee line near the CTA
7. Paired the 5-star rating with a supporting trust badge, since it's currently backed by 2 reviews

Same product, same brand, same price. Just put the reasons to buy before the decisions to make.

DM me "AUDIT" if you want me to do this for your store.

#ShopifyDesign #CRO #eCommerce #ShopifyDeveloper #ConversionOptimization #ProductPage #Shopify #UXDesign

caption:
Most DTC brands run one funnel for everyone.

Cold traffic who's never heard of you. Warm audiences who've visited your store three times. First-time browsers. People who've added to cart and left.

Same product page. Same ask. Same result: conversions that should've happened, didn't.

The fix isn't better creatives. It's building the right path for each type of person.

Here's the framework 👇

—

UNAWARE (cold traffic)
They don't know the problem exists. An ad interrupted their scroll and they have zero context.

→ Meta Ad → Advertorial → Product Page → Checkout

The advertorial does the heavy lifting. Story first, problem reveal, then your product as the answer. By the time they hit your PDP, they're not strangers — they understand why they need this.

—

PROBLEM AWARE (cool traffic)
They feel it. Hair thinning, never sleeping well, skin not clearing. They know something's off but haven't found what fixes it.

→ Meta Ad → Listicle → Product Page → Checkout

A listicle validates their frustration, names the solutions, and puts yours in the mix. They click through already half-convinced.

—

SOLUTION AWARE (warm traffic)
They've compared options. They've tried things. They know solutions exist — they just haven't committed to yours.

→ Meta Ad → Landing Page → Checkout

A dedicated landing page makes one case: why your product beats everything they've already considered. This is where the comparison gets won or lost.

—

MOST AWARE (hot traffic)
They've seen your ads. Been to your store. The trust is already there.

→ Meta Ad → Product Page → Checkout

Skip the education. Send them straight to the PDP with a strong offer. Every extra step is a leak.

—

The rule: the shorter the gap between where your customer is mentally and what you're asking them to do, the higher your conversion rate.

Most brands send everyone to the same page. The ones building funnels that match awareness levels are the ones winning on Meta right now.

Which audience is your current ad targeting?

caption:
The listicle is one of the most underused pages in eCommerce funnels.

Most brands don't build them. The ones that do usually hand them off to a content writer who treats it like a blog post, no CTA flow, no before/after, no conversion architecture.

A listicle done properly does two things at once:

First: it earns organic search traffic on problem-aware queries ("why does my cutting board smell", "is my cutting board making me sick"). These are people who know they have a problem but don't have a solution yet. They're searching with intent.

Second: it moves those people from awareness to purchase without feeling like a sales pitch. They're reading an article. The article happens to introduce your product as the answer to the exact problem they searched for.

This is the KURA listicle, built on my li-03 template. The headline: "5 Problems Your Cutting Board Is Causing Right Now."

Each problem block follows the same structure: agitate the pain, show what changes, introduce the mechanism. Then the page pivots. Transformation strip. Social proof. Final CTA.

Two-column alternating layout on desktop. Full single-column collapse on mobile. Inline CTAs at the highest-friction moments. Review cards from real-feeling customers.

Editorial at the top. Conversion funnel at the bottom.

If your store is running paid traffic to a product page and wondering why it doesn't convert, this is the page you're missing.

caption:
Material Kitchen makes some of the best-looking kitchen gear I've come across.

And their homepage still leaves sales on the table.

Here's what you get when you land on it on mobile: a beautiful hero photo, a headline, and one button that says "Shop The MK Free Collection."

That's the whole above-the-fold. No price. No rating. No proof. The "free shipping, 30-day trial, guaranteed for life" part is real — but it's stuck in a tiny bar at the very top that nobody reads. And on a fresh visit, a full-screen email popup can drop over all of it before you've seen anything.

So a first-time buyer is quietly asking "is this actually any good?" and the page hands them nothing to hold onto until they've scrolled past about 12,000 pixels of it.

I rebuilt the above-the-fold. Same brand, same photo, same fonts. All I did was move the selling to where the eye already is:

- Killed the popup so the hero shows straight away
- Put a real 5-star customer quote right under the headline
- Pulled the guarantee, trial and shipping into visible trust chips
- Surfaced a real bestseller with its real price ($195, down from $225)
- Made the button carry the offer instead of a vague "shop"

None of this is a redesign. The store was already gorgeous. The fix was clearing the path and putting proof, price and trust in front of people before they go looking for it.

If your store looks great but the sales don't match, this is usually the reason.

— Ridwan

caption:
Your store's animations aren't making it look premium. They're making it convert worse.

I know that's not what you want to hear after a weekend of adding scroll effects.

Here's the trap most Shopify brands fall into: more motion feels more high-end, and high-end feels like it should sell more. So they animate everything.

But motion isn't free. Amazon found that every 100ms of extra delay cost them about 1% in sales. Animations are the easiest way to add that delay without realising it.

The fix is to treat motion as a budget, not decoration. You get a small amount of attention and speed to spend on a page. Every animation spends some of it, so it has to buy something back.

Where it actually earns its place:

Selection feedback, so a shopper trusts their variant or bundle registered.
Add-to-cart confirmation, right when money is on the line.

Bebemoss sells a $44 crocheted bunny. No discount codes, no countdown timers, no "10,000 reviews" banner slapped across the page.

So I set myself a rule: build 4 ad directions for one of their toys and don't invent a single claim.

Where each one came from:

Problem: most "first toys" are plastic and in a landfill before the kid starts school. This one gets kept.

Benefit: GOTS organic cotton, crocheted by hand, made to EU toy-safety standards. Real specs, no filler.

Social proof: one actual review, "she's actually a work of art." Plus their 4.9 from wholesale buyers on Faire.

Offer: they have no sale to run, so I told the truth instead. It's made to order, by hand. That's the reason to act, not a fake timer.

Same bunny. Same photo. Four different reasons to care, depending on where the buyer's head is when they see it.

That's most of the job with ad creative. Not "make it pop." Figure out what the person needs to hear first.

Concept work. I'm not affiliated with Bebemoss, I just liked the product enough to think about how I'd sell it.

Everything else on the page just clears the path between those three.

Save this for your next funnel build.

Material Kitchen's Trio of Knives sits at a 5.0 rating from 472 reviews. I wanted to see how many honest angles I could pull out of that one product page.

Four ad directions, same three knives, nothing invented.

Problem: most people own a bulky 12-piece knife set and only ever reach for two blades in it. The Trio replaces the whole block with three full-tang, Japanese-steel knives.

Benefit: full-tang balance, a 13-degree edge, cryogenic tempering, and that 472-review rating. All of it is on their own product page, I didn't add anything.

Social proof: I could have written a testimonial that sounded better. Instead I used a real one, from a verified buyer named Mara T.: "Sleek design, perfect weight, and very sharp. I love them."

Offer: the set is actually $30 off right now, $225 down to $195, so the urgency ad leans on a real discount instead of a countdown timer that resets every week.

Four ads, one product, four different reasons to buy it depending on what the person scrolling past already believes.

The job here was picking which true fact to lead with for each kind of shopper.

This is concept work. I have no relationship with Material Kitchen, I just liked the knives enough to think through how I'd sell them.

Ridwan

Obvi has over 800,000 customers and a best seller sitting at 1,489 reviews.

The biggest words on their mobile homepage say "BACK IN STOCK."

That is a warehouse update. It only lands for someone who already tried to buy and got told no. Everyone else, which on a homepage fed by paid social is nearly everyone, reads the largest text on the screen and learns nothing about what the product does.

The part that would actually sell is right underneath at 13px, welded into one 40 word sentence. Metabolism, cravings, weight loss, hair, skin and nails, all in a single breath. Four real reasons to buy and not one of them scannable.

Then there is the bit I had to zoom in on to believe. The accessibility widget renders on top of the bottom left corner of the SHOP NOW button. Tap a little low and you get a settings panel instead of the store.

So I rebuilt the top of the page. Same pink, same purple, same wordmark, same product photo.

Headline states the outcome, using Obvi's own line from further down their page.
"Back in stock" moved to a small pill where it still works for returning buyers.
The paragraph became four benefit lines you can read in a second.
The 800,000 customer proof got weight instead of grey 11px type.
One primary button carrying the real offer, quiz demoted to a link under it.
The real best seller pulled up with its real price of $29.74 and its real 1,489 reviews.
Widget moved clear of every tap target.

Nothing was redesigned. The brand was already doing its job. The hero was just spending its biggest slot announcing inventory.

Quick test for your own homepage. If the headline would still make sense written on a warehouse whiteboard, it is not selling.

caption:
You think more trust badges build more trust. That's exactly what's making shoppers bounce.

You spent an afternoon adding every trust signal you could find. Secure checkout badge. Money-back guarantee. As seen in. Free shipping banner. Verified reviews widget. All stacked above the fold.

Conversion didn't move. If anything it got worse.

Here's the part nobody tells you: past a certain number, trust badges stop reading as proof and start reading as defense. A wall of logos doesn't say "you can trust us." It says "something here needs explaining."

I see this on Shopify product pages constantly. Founders keep adding badges because each one feels safe on its own. Stacked together they read as anxious.

The fix isn't zero trust signals. It's one real one, said clearly.

One specific review with a name and a photo beats five generic star ratings.
Your actual return policy in plain words beats a "guarantee" badge.
A real founder photo beats a "featured in" logo strip.
Cut until only the signals answering a real objection are left.

Every page is a product. Every click is a choice. Stop performing trust. Start earning it.

Save this before your next PDP audit.

caption:
Your PDP loses sales at 60% scroll, not at the hero.

Most advice tells you to fix above the fold. New photography. Rewritten headline. Faster page speed.

But your buyers aren't leaving at the top.

They scroll past your beautiful hero image, and somewhere in the middle of the page, they hit a wall. The size guide is buried. The specs are unformatted. The guarantee is in the footer. They decide this isn't worth figuring out, and they leave.

Here's how to zone your PDP and fix it:

→ Zone 1 (0–40%): Hero zone. Hook, product image, primary CTA. Stop the scroll.
→ Zone 2 (40–70%): Decision zone. Size guide, specs, social proof, trust signals. This is where you close.
→ Zone 3 (70–100%): Reinforcement zone. Reviews, cross-sells, secondary CTA.

Most Shopify PDPs fail in Zone 2.

Not because the product is bad. Because the decision elements are in the wrong place, in the wrong format, at the wrong scroll depth.

Restructure Zone 2 before you touch anything else.

Save this for your next PDP audit. Share it with a Shopify store owner who needs it.

73% of Shopify redesigns don't lift conversions.

Not because the design was bad.
Because the wrong problem was solved.

Most store owners jump straight to Figma. New hero image. Bigger fonts. Trending layout. It looks cleaner. But conversion barely moves.

Here's what's actually missing — The Conversion Layer.

It's the strategic audit you run before a single pixel moves. Three questions answer everything:

→ Clarify: What does this page need to communicate? What's the buyer's one burning question?
→ Construct: Does the layout follow the buyer's journey — or your designer's preference?
→ Convert: What's the single action this page must drive? Is every element pointing there?

That's the 3C Framework.

Before I open Figma on any CRO project, I run this. 15 minutes of diagnosis saves 3 weeks of redesign that doesn't move the needle.

The Conversion Layer isn't a style choice. It's a strategic brief. And it's the difference between a page that looks better and a page that sells more.

caption:
Bebemoss makes handmade toys. Every one crocheted by a woman artisan, a lot of them refugees. I like the brand, which is exactly why the collection page bothered me.

It opens with five sentences about the mission. On a phone that block is 519px tall and the screen is 844, so the whole first screen is copy. The first toy creeps in at the bottom edge with its name and price still cut off.

Nobody taps "Soft Toys" to read a mission statement. They tap it to see toys.

Two other things while I was in there.

A pink "Save 10%" tab is docked to the bottom left. The page runs 8,200px and that tab rides the whole way down. On my screen it sat right on top of a toy's name and price.

And there are 48 products with no filter and no sort. Bebemoss already names its ranges in its own copy, Safari, Ocean, Woodland, Garden Life, Dreams. None of that is something a shopper can tap.

So I rebuilt the top of the page. Same photos, same prices, same brand.

- Mission down to one line, with a "Read our story" link for anyone who wants the rest
- Those five ranges as filter chips, price sort sitting next to them
- Grid starts at the fold, four toys with names and prices before you scroll
- Save pill shrunk and moved bottom right, clear of the card text

The story still sells. It just sells better standing next to the toys instead of in front of them.

If your collection page opens with a paragraph, go look at it on your phone right now.

Ridwan

caption:
Your store isn't mobile optimised. It just fits the screen.

Those are two different things, and only one of them sells.

Responsive means your layout reflows at 390px wide.

It says nothing about whether a thumb can reach the button.

Here is the test most owners run. Phone in both hands, at a desk, good light. Everything looks fine.

Here is the real one. One hand, standing on a bus, thumb anchored bottom right.

Now pick a size, set a quantity, and buy.

Apple has published a 44pt minimum tap target for years. Google says 48dp.

Measure your swatches against that before you argue with me.

What I keep finding on Shopify product pages:

Add to cart that only exists above the fold.
Variant swatches sized for a mouse cursor.
Filters parked in the top left, the hardest corner for a right thumb.
Quantity steppers you have to aim at.

None of that needs a redesign to fix.

Move the decisions into the bottom third. Make them big enough to hit without looking.

Every page is a product. Every click is a choice. Make the choice easy to hit.

Save this and test your own PDP tonight.

caption:
Gainful asks you four questions before it gives you one reason to trust it.

Their protein customizer is a good idea. Pick a dietary preference, pick a goal, get a formula matched to it. On mobile it opens with two different 25% discounts stacked on top of each other, one for subscribing and one for a new customer code, and nothing on the page tells you whether they stack or which one you should take.

Then it asks for four decisions. Dietary preference. Primary goal. Serving size. Flavour packets.

And it never offers you a way to buy.

I searched every button and link on that page. There is no add to cart. No buy button. No checkout. The only call to action anywhere is Take The Quiz, sitting 3,693 pixels down, and it sends you into a different funnel than the one you were already halfway through.

The words guarantee, money back, cancel anytime and risk free do not appear on the page either. That last one matters, because the loudest thing on the screen is asking you to start a subscription.

So I rebuilt the top of it. Same type, same warm grey, same black pills, same photography.

One promo strip instead of two, and the subscribe offer moved down to the buy area where it is an actual choice.
Price given its own line at 29px with a per serving figure under it, because on a configurator the price is the running total.
A sticky bar carrying the live price and an add to cart, so the endpoint is visible from the first tap.
Cancel or skip anytime, sitting right where the subscription is being asked for.
The review count turned into a link you can actually check.
One line above the two selectors naming what they produce.

Nothing invented. Every number is Gainful's own, read off the live page: $31.47, 14 servings, 20g protein, 100 calories, 6 ingredients, 2,123 ratings.

If your page asks the shopper to do work, it owes them somewhere to put it.

Ridwan

The review quote in the rebuild is an illustrative placeholder, labelled as such in the file, not a real Gainful customer.

caption:
3 types of buyers land on your Shopify store.

Cold traffic doesn't know your brand.
Warm traffic is comparing you to alternatives.
Hot traffic has mentally decided. They just need to click.

You're showing all three the same page.

When CVR looks flat, the instinct is to fix the page. But a page converting 8% of hot buyers and 0.5% of cold ones averages to around 2%. That number isn't telling you the page is broken. It's telling you the routing is wrong.

Here's what each stage actually needs:

→ Cold traffic: Proof before product. Social proof above the fold. Problem-first copy that names their situation before naming your solution. Brand context in two sentences.

→ Warm traffic: Comparison, not persuasion. They're in research mode, evaluating you against the obvious alternative. Give them a comparison table, benefit-led copy, and reviews that answer the objection they're holding.

→ Hot traffic: A path, not a pitch. Buy button above the fold. Genuine urgency if you have it. Nothing between their intent and the checkout.

The routing fix:
Cold traffic → pre-sell page or quiz funnel (not your PDP)
Warm retargeting → full social-proof PDP
Cart abandons → stripped offer page, one button

Your next CRO win probably isn't on the product page. It's in knowing which buyer you're actually talking to.

caption:
Cold traffic doesn't bounce because your page is ugly. It's missing one of 5 parts.

You wrote a pre-sell page. It reads like an ad.

Cold traffic can smell an ad in one line. They leave before they ever see your product.

Here's the part most Shopify brands skip. A pre-sell page is not one big pitch. It's a sequence. Five parts, each doing one job.

The Hook, which earns permission to keep reading.

The Mirror, which says their frustration back to them.

The Discovery, which introduces your mechanism like it was found.

The Proof Layer, real numbers, not adjectives.

The Soft Bridge, which hands them to the product without pitching.

Skip one part and the whole thing collapses.

Straight to a PDP, cold traffic converts near 1 to 2%. Run it through this sequence first and that number moves.

This is the conversion layer between your ad and your product page.

Save this before you write your next pre-sell page. Want it audited? My DMs are open.

caption:
TAPro's homepage never shows a price, a star rating, or a single product. Not on the first screen.

TAPro sells NFC and QR review cards to local businesses. Land on their homepage and you get a promo banner and a big hero photo. Scroll past that, past a full video demo, and you still won't see a product or a price.

Keep scrolling into a product grid and you'll hit their flagship card, the G-Series Onyx: $34.95, a real 4.9 star rating from 1,125 reviews, and over 15,500 businesses using their cards, including names like Sheraton and McDonald's. All of it real. None of it near the top.

Here's what I changed and why:

1. Pulled the real price and 4.9 star rating up, directly under the headline
2. Put the actual product front and center, a real photo instead of a placeholder
3. Pulled the "15,500+ businesses" trust strip up from deep in the page
4. Collapsed the two-row promo banner into one thin line
5. Removed a duplicate search icon overlapping the headline
6. Pointed the CTA at that one flagship product instead of a generic banner link

Same brand, same product, same price. Just put the proof where a first-time visitor can actually see it.

DM me "AUDIT" if you want this done for your store.

caption:
Your headline got bigger. The page still feels flat.

I did this for years. Client says the page feels muddy, I bump the H1, they still say it feels muddy. So I bump the subhead so it doesn't look orphaned. Then the price, so it doesn't get lost. Two rounds later everything is bigger and nothing leads.

Here's what I had wrong. Hierarchy is a ranking, not a size. Six things set at 32px is not six levels. It's one level, printed six times.

Nielsen Norman Group put the number on it: on an average visit, people read at most about 28% of the words on a page. They are not reading. They are scanning for the one thing that wins. If your page doesn't hand them a winner in two seconds, they pick one for you, and it's rarely the one you wanted.

So I stopped counting sizes and started assigning jobs. Six levels, six jobs:

1. Page promise, the outcome
2. Section signpost, where am I
3. Block claim, why this part
4. Body, the proof
5. Action, the button
6. Fine print, the risk

If a level has no job, it isn't a level. Delete it.

And the part most people skip: two of those six levels can be pure space. Same type sizes, different gaps, and suddenly the page reads. Nothing had to get bigger. Things just had to stop touching.

Quick test before you ship. Look at your product page at arm's length and squint. Name what you see first. If you can't do it in two seconds, you don't have a hierarchy problem you can solve with font sizes.

Design isn't decoration, it's direction.

Repost if your last redesign ended with everything one step bigger.

caption:
Product Page (PDP) audit: Caraway's Fry Pan, on mobile.

You think 18,886 reviews means the trust is already there.

It doesn't, if the page can't render them in time.

Real findings, nothing invented:

The price sits top-right, aligned with the review line, disconnected from the title above it. On a fresh load, that review line can paint as the bare word "Reviews" with no stars and no count, right next to the price, exactly when a shopper is deciding if $125 is worth it. And depending on what's loaded above it, the product photo itself can land past the fold.

The rebuild moves price directly under the title, renders stars and count inline every time, and gives the real product photo (background removed, composited on a dark surface) the whole first screen.

Same product. Same price. The only thing that changed is the order the page tells its own story in.

Full before/after and annotated breakdown in the carousel.

Repost if this is useful to someone building a product page right now.

caption:
PRODUCT PAGE (PDP): Kyte Baby's Sleep Bag in Oat 1.0 already had 29,067 five-star reviews and real safety certifications above the fold. Then the buy button rendered flat gray, no size selected, reading as disabled at the exact moment a shopper was ready to act.

The fix wasn't more proof. The proof was already there. It was the button.

Three changes:
1. Recolored the CTA to high-contrast red. Never gray, never looks disabled.
2. Moved shipping, returns, and Afterpay right under the button instead of a full scroll away, buried below a temperature slider.
3. Called out the AAP-compliant and OEKO-TEX certifications as benefit chips, not buried copy.

Same product. Same reviews. A button that finally matches the trust the page already earned.

This is unofficial portfolio work, not a Kyte Baby engagement. Repost if you've ever shipped a page that proved itself right up until the button.
